newsitem.title: USA: U.S. envoy upbeat on Guatemala economic prospects.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy upbeat on Guatemala economic prospects.

text.p: The end of decades of civil war in Guatemela heralds a new era of economic opportunity, the U.S. ambassador to the Central American country said on Wednesday.
The climate for foreign investors is bright, particularly in the telecommunications and electronics sectors, ambassador Donald Planty said.
An international aid package of $2.5 billion is expected to be put together, and much of it will be spent on repairing and improving the infrastructure, Planty said.
"We're very excited by the prospects for Guatemala's future," he told a briefing for businessmen at the Miami Conference on the Caribbean and Latin America.
"We believe Guatemala is poised to take off as an economy. We will see Guatemala move ahead very quickly."

The peace accords end more than 36 years of war between leftist guerrillas and various governments, often military regimes. More than 100,000 people were killed, mostly civilians, and 40,000 have "disappeared".

The final agreement will be signed in Guatemala City on Dec. 29. In January the international community meets in Brussels to discuss an aid package which should total $2.5 billion, of which the United Statets will offer $250 million.

Planty said the accords went further than simply ending the fighting. They were a "blueprint for the future" which spelt out a series of social and political reforms, including reducing the power of the military whose past actions made Guatemala an international pariah.
Major work is needed on the infrastructure, which suffered badly in the war. Bridges and roads were a priority.
A prime opportunity for foreign investors is in telecommunications and electronics, Planty said. The telecommunications sector is being privatised and vast areas of the country are without amenities.
He said that the government was keen for foreign investment but was realistic about how much it might attract.
"They are not counting on an investment boom to bring them out of their situation," he said.
Foreign companies would find President Alvaro Arzu's government eager to work with them, Planty said.
"We think this is the best goverment Guatemala has had in anyone's memory."
On the downside, crime, including kidnappings, is rife.
The workforce badly needs to be modernised with better education and training, he said.
